labs.title: Server Naming
labs.subTitle: DC01 · Windows Server 2025
labs.task: Rename the Windows Server to a standardised hostname before configuring Active Directory.

blocks.text: Renamed the computer through Server Manager → Local Server → Computer Name → System Properties. The default Windows-generated hostname was replaced with DC01, and the server was restarted to apply the change.
PowerShell equivalent
Rename-Computer -NewName DC01 -Restart
Renamed the Windows Server to DC01 to establish a clear naming convention before installing Active Directory Domain Services and promoting the server to a Domain Controller.
Confirmed after the restart that Server Manager → Local Server displayed the computer name as DC01.

blocks.text: Renamed each Windows 11 workstation through Settings → System → Rename. Each client was restarted after the hostname change was applied.

Renamed the two Windows 11 Pro workstations from their default Windows-generated hostnames to CLIENT01 and CLIENT02.
Using standardised hostnames makes the systems easier to identify and manage as they are later joined to the Active Directory domain.

labs.title: Static IPv4 Configuration
labs.subTitle: DC01 · 192.168.11.10/24
labs.task: Configure a static IPv4 address on DC01 before installing Active Directory Domain Services.

blocks.text: Configured the static address using PowerShell in an elevated session:

New-NetIPAddress -InterfaceAlias "Ethernet0" -IPAddress 192.168.11.10 -PrefixLength 24 -DefaultGateway 192.168.11.2

Set-DnsClientServerAddress -InterfaceAlias "Ethernet0" -ServerAddresses 127.0.0.1

Configured DC01 with a static IPv4 address so the server maintains a consistent network address. A stable IP address is important for a Domain Controller because client computers will later depend on it for services such as Active Directory authentication and DNS.
Selected 192.168.11.10 to keep the Domain Controller outside the VMware DHCP address pool (192.168.11.128 to 192.168.11.254) and prevent potential IP conflicts with dynamically assigned addresses.
The VMware DHCP range was verified through Virtual Network Editor → VMnet8 → DHCP Settings.
Verified the final network configuration in PowerShell using:
ipconfig /all
The output confirmed the host name DC01, DHCP disabled, the IPv4 address 192.168.11.10, subnet mask 255.255.255.0, default gateway 192.168.11.2 and DNS server 127.0.0.1.

blocks.caption: Before: Server Manager showing Ethernet0 with an IPv4 address assigned by DHCP.
After: ipconfig /all on DC01 confirming the static configuration.

blocks.text: This screenshot carries deliberate redactions for identifiers that serve no purpose in a public portfolio: the MAC address, link-local IPv6 address, DHCPv6 IAID and DHCPv6 Client DUID. The original unedited capture is retained privately. Supporting evidence of the VMware VMnet8 DHCP settings, showing subnet 192.168.11.0/24 with a pool of .128 to .254, is also retained privately.

labs.title: Connectivity Verification & Troubleshooting
labs.subTitle: Firewall profiles · ARP cache
labs.task: Verify two-way IPv4 connectivity between DC01 and both Windows 11 client systems before installing Active Directory Domain Services, and troubleshoot any communication failures.

blocks.text: Initial client-to-server test
Tested IPv4 connectivity from CLIENT01 to DC01:

The initial test returned Request timed out with 100% packet loss. Windows Defender Firewall with Advanced Security was checked on DC01, and the inbound rule File and Printer Sharing (Echo Request - ICMPv4-In) was enabled to permit ICMPv4 Echo Requests. The test was repeated from CLIENT01 and connectivity to DC01 succeeded.

CLIENT02 was then tested against the same destination. The test succeeded without requiring a firewall change on CLIENT02, because the ICMP request was outbound from CLIENT02 and the relevant inbound firewall rule had already been enabled on the destination, DC01.
Reverse connectivity test
Connectivity was then tested in the opposite direction, from DC01 toward the Windows 11 clients:
The initial DC01 → CLIENT01 test failed.
Firewall profile investigation on CLIENT01
Windows Defender Firewall with Advanced Security was inspected on CLIENT01. Multiple instances of the File and Printer Sharing (Echo Request - ICMPv4-In) rule existed for different firewall profiles:

Because CLIENT01 had not yet been joined to the Active Directory domain, the enabled Domain-profile rule did not apply to its current network profile. The appropriate Private/Public ICMPv4 inbound rule was enabled.
ARP troubleshooting

After correcting the firewall profile configuration on CLIENT01, another connectivity test from DC01 produced a different failure: Destination host unreachable. This was different from the earlier Request timed out result.
Because the correct client-side firewall rule was already enabled, the ARP cache on DC01 was cleared to remove stale address-resolution information:
arp -d *

Connectivity was then tested again and the test succeeded with 0% packet loss. The appropriate ICMPv4 inbound rule was also enabled on CLIENT02, and reverse connectivity from DC01 was verified successfully.
Two distinct connectivity failure modes were encountered and treated separately.
1. Request timed out

The initial CLIENT01 → DC01 test returned Request timed out. The issue was resolved by enabling the required inbound ICMPv4 Echo Request rule on the destination system, DC01. This demonstrated that although basic IP addressing was configured correctly, the destination firewall still controlled whether the server would respond to ICMP diagnostic traffic.

During later reverse testing from DC01 → CLIENT01, firewall profile scope also became important. On CLIENT01 the Domain-scoped ICMPv4 rule was already enabled, while the applicable Private/Public-scoped rule was disabled. Because the client had not yet joined the domain, enabling or relying on the Domain rule did not permit the traffic. Enabling the rule associated with the client's active firewall profile corrected that portion of the configuration.
2. Destination host unreachable

After the correct client-side firewall rule was enabled, DC01 later returned Destination host unreachable. This represented a different failure from a firewall timeout. At that stage the firewall configuration had already been corrected, and stale ARP information on DC01 was preventing the server from correctly resolving the client's Layer 2 address.

The ARP cache was cleared with arp -d * and a subsequent ping succeeded, confirming that the corrected firewall configuration was working and that stale ARP information had been masking the successful fix.
Firewall directionality

The tests also demonstrated firewall directionality. CLIENT02 → DC01 succeeded without making an inbound firewall change on CLIENT02, because the traffic originated from the client and was received by DC01. For the reverse test, DC01 to CLIENT02, the relevant inbound ICMPv4 rule needed to be permitted on CLIENT02, because CLIENT02 was now the destination receiving the Echo Request.
Security consideration

ICMP Echo Requests were enabled deliberately for lab diagnostics and connectivity verification. Allowing ICMP is not automatically appropriate in every production environment. Production firewall configuration should follow organisational security policy and may restrict ICMP according to firewall profile, source network, destination, administrative requirements and network-monitoring requirements.

Rather than disabling Windows Defender Firewall entirely, only the specific inbound functionality required for the diagnostic tests was enabled. This preserved the firewall as a security control while allowing the connectivity testing required by the lab.
Firewall profile investigation

labs.title: Active Directory Domain Services Installation & Domain Controller Promotion
labs.subTitle: DC01 · corp.gracelab.com
labs.task: Install Active Directory Domain Services on DC01, create a new Active Directory forest, and promote DC01 to the first Domain Controller for the corp.gracelab.com domain.

blocks.text: DNS client configuration
Before promoting DC01, its preferred DNS server was changed from the loopback address 127.0.0.1 to its own static IPv4 address, so that the server queries the DNS service it is about to host.
PowerShell equivalent
Set-DnsClientServerAddress -InterfaceAlias "Ethernet0" -ServerAddresses 192.168.11.10
Role installation

Active Directory Domain Services and the DNS Server role were installed through Server Manager. After installation, DC01 was confirmed to still be a member of WORKGROUP, establishing the pre-promotion state.
PowerShell equivalent

Install-WindowsFeature -Name AD-Domain-Services -IncludeManagementTools
Install-WindowsFeature -Name DNS -IncludeManagementTools
Domain controller promotion

The Active Directory Domain Services Configuration Wizard was used to add a new forest with the root domain name corp.gracelab.com. The NetBIOS name CORP was assigned automatically. DNS Server and Global Catalog were enabled, and a Directory Services Restore Mode password was configured.

During the DNS Options stage the wizard reported that a DNS delegation could not be created. No delegation was configured, because the environment contains no authoritative parent zone for corp.gracelab.com.
Before the installation was started, the wizard's View Script option was used to inspect the PowerShell equivalent of the selected configuration.
Generated by the wizard

Install-ADDSForest `
  -DomainName "corp.gracelab.com" `
  -DomainNetbiosName "CORP" `
  -DomainMode "Win2025" `
  -ForestMode "Win2025" `
  -InstallDns:$true `
  -CreateDnsDelegation:$false
The prerequisites check completed successfully and DC01 restarted automatically once promotion finished.
DC01 was configured to use 192.168.11.10 as its preferred DNS server because Active Directory relies on DNS to locate domain controllers and the services they advertise.

The corp.gracelab.com DNS zone was not created manually before promotion. DNS configuration for the new forest was allowed to occur as part of the Active Directory deployment. After promotion, the resulting zone was verified rather than assumed to be correct, and was found to be a Primary, Active Directory integrated zone configured for Secure dynamic updates. No remediation was required.

The DNS delegation warning shown during promotion was expected. The environment contains no parent DNS infrastructure from which corp.gracelab.com would need to be delegated, so there was no delegation for the wizard to create. The warning does not indicate a failed promotion.

The generated script contained -InstallDns:$true, confirming that DNS installation and configuration were included in the forest promotion even though the DNS Server role had already been installed manually. The View Script option also demonstrates that the configuration wizard is a graphical interface over the Install-ADDSForest deployment process.
Functional level

The domain and forest were created directly at the Windows Server 2025 functional level. This is appropriate here because every domain controller in the forest is built on Windows Server 2025. Functional levels can be raised but never lowered, and at this level no earlier Windows Server release can ever serve as a domain controller in the forest. In production this choice would require compatibility planning before deployment.
Firewall profile transition

Before promotion, Server Manager showed DC01 using the Public firewall profile. After promotion, Windows Network Location Awareness classified the network as DomainAuthenticated, which was verified with Get-NetConnectionProfile.

This connects directly to the firewall troubleshooting carried out during connectivity testing. Before the domain existed, Domain scoped firewall rules did not apply to systems operating under the Public or Private profiles. Once DC01 became a domain controller and the network authenticated against the domain, the Domain profile became the applicable one.
Domain controller state
Server Manager, Local Server showed the computer name DC01 with the domain corp.gracelab.com in place of the previous WORKGROUP membership, and the firewall profile reported as Domain.
Directory and DNS
Active Directory Users and Computers showed DC01 inside the Domain Controllers organizational unit with a DC Type of GC, confirming global catalog configuration.
Get-DnsServerZone -Name "corp.gracelab.com" | Format-List ZoneName, ZoneType, IsDsIntegrated, DynamicUpdate
Domain and forest

Get-ADDomain | Select-Object DNSRoot, NetBIOSName, DomainMode, PDCEmulator | Format-List
Get-ADForest | Select-Object RootDomain, ForestMode, SchemaMaster, DomainNamingMaster | Format-List
Domain controller health

dcdiag /test:Advertising /test:SysVolCheck /test:NetLogons /test:RidManager | Select-String "passed test|failed test"
net share

Connectivity, Advertising, SysVolCheck, NetLogons and RidManager all passed. The Connectivity test appears in the results without being explicitly requested, because dcdiag runs it automatically as a prerequisite for every targeted test. The NETLOGON and SYSVOL shares were both present, confirming that DC01 was advertising as a domain controller, that SYSVOL was initialised, that Netlogon was functioning and that RID allocation was healthy.

blocks.caption: DC01 configured with 192.168.11.10 as both its static IPv4 address and preferred DNS server, before promotion.
AD DS and DNS roles installed while DC01 was still a member of WORKGROUP.
The wizard's View Script output showing the generated Install-ADDSForest configuration.
After the automatic restart, Server Manager shows DC01 as a member of corp.gracelab.com and the active firewall profile changed from Public to Domain.
Get-NetConnectionProfile confirming the network classified as DomainAuthenticated, with the available firewall profiles listed.
Active Directory Users and Computers showing DC01 in the Domain Controllers organizational unit with a DC Type of GC.
The corp.gracelab.com zone verified as a Primary, Active Directory integrated zone using Secure dynamic updates.
Get-ADDomain confirming the DNS domain name, NetBIOS name, Windows Server 2025 domain functional level and PDC Emulator role.
Get-ADForest confirming the forest root, Windows Server 2025 forest functional level, Schema Master and Domain Naming Master.
Targeted dcdiag tests passing, and net share confirming the NETLOGON and SYSVOL shares.

labs.title: Domain Join & Domain Discovery Troubleshooting
labs.subTitle: CLIENT01 & CLIENT02 · DNS, credentials, NLA
labs.task: Join CLIENT01 and CLIENT02 to the corp.gracelab.com domain, and verify on each system that domain membership, the computer account secure channel, and the network location classification are all correct.

blocks.text: Pre-join baseline

Before any configuration change was made on CLIENT01, the existing network classification was recorded, so that the post-join state could be compared against a known starting point. This value cannot be recovered once a system has been joined.
Get-NetConnectionProfile
The connection was classified as Public with a DomainAuthenticationKind of None.
Deliberate domain join failure

The domain join was attempted on CLIENT01 before DNS reconfiguration, in order to observe and document the failure mode. The attempt returned that an Active Directory Domain Controller for the domain corp.gracelab.com could not be contacted.
The Details view of the error was expanded to obtain the underlying diagnostic information:

The query was for the SRV record for _ldap._tcp.dc._msdcs.corp.gracelab.com
The error was: "No records found for given DNS query."
(error code 0x0000251D DNS_INFO_NO_RECORDS)
DNS diagnosis and correction
Get-NetIPConfiguration -InterfaceAlias "Ethernet0"

The output showed a working DHCP assigned address of 192.168.11.130 with a preferred DNS server of 192.168.11.2, the VMware NAT gateway. That resolver has no knowledge of the corp.gracelab.com namespace.
The preferred DNS server was changed to the domain controller and the resolver cache was cleared. The IPv4 address was deliberately left on DHCP, because the address assignment was not the fault.
PowerShell equivalent

Set-DnsClientServerAddress -InterfaceAlias "Ethernet0" -ServerAddresses 192.168.11.10
ipconfig /flushdns
Domain controller discovery
Before retrying the join, domain controller discovery was tested directly. The same lookup that had previously returned no records now resolved successfully.
nltest /dsgetdc:corp.gracelab.com
The command returned DC01.corp.gracelab.com at 192.168.11.10, together with the advertised service flags PDC, GC, LDAP, KDC, TIMESERV and WRITABLE.
Domain join and credential scope
Add-Computer -DomainName "corp.gracelab.com" -Credential (Get-Credential) -Restart

The first attempt failed reporting that the user name or password was incorrect. The account name had been entered as Administrator without a domain qualifier, which resolved against the local account database on CLIENT01 rather than against the domain. The attempt was repeated using CORP\Administrator and completed successfully. The password was never incorrect.
Authentication availability at sign-in

After the restart, the first sign-in attempt as CORP\Administrator failed because the domain was not available. DC01 was found to be powered off. The domain controller was started, and the sign-in then completed successfully.
Domain join of CLIENT02

CLIENT02 was configured with the correct DNS server before any join attempt and joined while DC01 was running, so that it could serve as a control case against CLIENT01. An initial attempt to change the DNS server from a standard session returned a PermissionDenied CIM error; the command was re-run from an elevated session and completed successfully.
Domain controller discovery depends on DNS service records

The failed join did not attempt to resolve a host named corp.gracelab.com. It queried DNS for the service location record _ldap._tcp.dc._msdcs.corp.gracelab.com, which is how a client discovers which servers advertise LDAP for a given domain. This process is known as the DC Locator.
Because the client was querying a resolver that is not authoritative for the Active Directory namespace, no such record existed and discovery failed before any authentication could be attempted.

The returned error code is significant. DNS_INFO_NO_RECORDS indicates that the DNS server responded and reported that it holds no matching record. It does not indicate that DNS was unreachable or that the query timed out. A resolver that is unavailable and a resolver that answers but is not authoritative are two different faults with two different remedies.
Client DNS requirements are not specific to a lab

Pointing domain clients at Active Directory integrated DNS is not a home lab convenience. Any domain joined client, in any environment, requires DNS that can resolve the Active Directory namespace, whether directly or through DNS infrastructure that forwards to it. A client configured to use a public resolver alone cannot locate a domain controller.
Credentials must be scoped to the domain

An unqualified account name is evaluated against the local account database of the machine performing the operation. Supplying CORP\Administrator, or the equivalent user principal name, scopes the credential to the domain instead.

The error combined both possible causes into a single message stating that the user name or password was incorrect. Windows reports these together deliberately, so that failed authentication attempts cannot be used to determine which account names exist. Both the credential scope and the password therefore had to be treated as candidate causes.
Authentication requires a reachable domain controller or a cached credential
The sign-in failure that followed the restart was not a configuration fault. DNS was correct and the credential was correct, but no domain controller was running to authenticate against.

Windows caches credential verifiers for recent successful domain sign-ins, so that a user who has previously signed in on a system can continue to do so while the domain is unavailable. No such cached verifier existed for CORP\Administrator on CLIENT01, because that account had never signed in on that machine, so the sign-in failed outright rather than falling back.

The local account on CLIENT01 remained usable throughout, because local accounts persist on a domain joined workstation. This differs from a domain controller, where the local account database is removed during promotion.
Domain membership and network classification are independent
After the successful join, CLIENT01 reported PartOfDomain as True and a computer account secure channel in good condition, while the network remained classified as Public.

These describe two different relationships. The secure channel is the trust between the computer account and the domain, maintained through the machine account password. The network classification is the assessment made by Network Location Awareness of the connection itself, and it determines which Windows Defender Firewall profile is applied.

Network Location Awareness classifies a connection when the network initialises and does not re-evaluate that classification on its own afterwards. CLIENT01 had started while DC01 was powered off, so no domain controller could be reached at classification time and the connection fell back to Public. The domain controller becoming available later did not alter the result. Restarting the client with the domain controller running produced a classification of DomainAuthenticated.

A correctly joined system with a healthy secure channel can still have every Domain scoped firewall rule fail to apply, while every check of the join itself returns a correct result. This continues the firewall behaviour examined during connectivity testing, where Domain scoped inbound rules did not apply to systems operating under the Private or Public profiles. The same mechanism is visible here from the opposite direction.
Control case

CLIENT02 was configured with the correct DNS server before any join attempt and was joined while DC01 was running. It classified as DomainAuthenticated on its first start, with no intervening restart. Applying the same procedure to two systems, with the availability of the domain controller at start-up as the only meaningful difference, isolates that condition as the cause of the classification observed on CLIENT01.

Get-CimInstance Win32_ComputerSystem | Select-Object Name, Domain, PartOfDomain
Get-NetConnectionProfile
Test-ComputerSecureChannel -Verbose

The secure channel result was identical before and after the corrective restart on CLIENT01. The value that did not change is what confirms the join itself was never the fault, and that only the network classification was incorrect.
Directory verification

On DC01, Active Directory Users and Computers was opened and the Computers container inspected. Both CLIENT01 and CLIENT02 were present as computer objects, confirming from the directory side what had been verified from each client.

blocks.caption: The network classification recorded before any configuration change, showing Public with no domain authentication.
The join attempted before DNS reconfiguration. The underlying dialog shows the domain name entered correctly and the system still a member of WORKGROUP.
The expanded diagnostic identifying the failed SRV record query and the DNS_INFO_NO_RECORDS result.
The client using the VMware NAT gateway as its preferred DNS server.
The same command after the change, with the preferred DNS server set to the domain controller. The IPv4 address remains DHCP assigned.
nltest locating DC01 at 192.168.11.10 with its advertised service flags, using the same lookup that had previously returned no records.
The join failing on an unqualified account name.
The sign-in screen scoped to CORP with the domain qualified account entered, and the existing local account still available.
The sign-in failing because no domain controller was reachable and no cached credential existed for that account on that system.
Domain membership confirmed and the secure channel in good condition, while the network remained classified as Public. This image combines two command outputs captured during the same session.
The same checks after restarting with the domain controller available, showing DomainAuthenticated classification and an unchanged secure channel result.

Domain membership, network classification and secure channel all confirmed on the first start after the join.

labs.title: OUs, Users, Groups & Remote Administration
labs.subTitle: corp.gracelab.com · AGDLP · RSAT
labs.task: Build a custom Organizational Unit structure for user, group and workstation administration, create departmental accounts and role based security groups, apply NTFS permissions to a shared folder using the AGDLP model, relocate the client computer objects and redirect where future domain joins land, then administer the directory from CLIENT01 through RSAT rather than from the domain controller.

config.value: IT, HR, Sales, beneath GraceLab › Users

blocks.text: Reviewing the default structure

Active Directory Users and Computers was opened on DC01 and Advanced Features was enabled, which exposes the Object and Security tabs used later in this lab and reveals system objects hidden by default. The domain was reviewed before anything was created.

The distinction is not presentational. A container cannot be the target of a Group Policy link and cannot receive delegated administrative control, so a custom Organizational Unit hierarchy was created rather than leaving objects in the default containers.
Organizational Unit structure

GraceLab was created at the domain root with four child Organizational Units, and three departmental Organizational Units beneath Users. Protect object from accidental deletion was left enabled on each, which is the default.

corp.gracelab.com
└── GraceLab
    ├── Users
    │   ├── IT
    │   ├── HR
    │   └── Sales
    ├── Workstations
    ├── Groups
    └── Disabled Users
PowerShell equivalent
The custom Users Organizational Unit and the default Users container coexist without conflict. They share a display name but differ in parent, distinguished name and object class.
User accounts

Six accounts were created directly in their departmental Organizational Units, each requiring a password change at next logon. That is the same flag a help desk password reset sets, so provisioning and reset behave identically at the client.
PowerShell equivalent

New-ADUser -Name "Daniel Carter" -GivenName "Daniel" -Surname "Carter" `
    -SamAccountName "dcarter" -UserPrincipalName "dcarter@corp.gracelab.com" `
    -Path "OU=IT,OU=Users,OU=GraceLab,DC=corp,DC=gracelab,DC=com" `
    -AccountPassword (Read-Host -AsSecureString "Password") `
    -ChangePasswordAtLogon $true -Enabled $true

Read-Host -AsSecureString was used in place of a literal so that no password value reaches a transcript, a command history or a screenshot. Each account carries three names: the common name shown in the tree, the sAMAccountName used for down-level logon, and the user principal name. A user reporting a fault gives the display name, a ticket gives the sAMAccountName, and the sign-in prompt accepts either the down-level or the user principal name form.
Naming standard audit
A verification query was run after creation, scoped to the whole domain rather than to the new Organizational Units, so that an account created in the wrong place would still be returned.

Get-ADUser -Filter * | Select-Object Name,SamAccountName,DistinguishedName |
    Sort-Object DistinguishedName

The built-in Administrator, Guest and krbtgt accounts remained in the default Users container while all six created accounts sat beneath GraceLab. The query also found a defect: the sAMAccountName for Jason Brooks had been created as JBROOKS against a lowercase standard. The value is not case sensitive for authentication, so the account would have signed in without difficulty, but it appears in every subsequent report. It was corrected before any group or permission work began.

Set-ADUser -Identity "JBROOKS" -SamAccountName "jbrooks" `
    -UserPrincipalName "jbrooks@corp.gracelab.com"
Changing the sAMAccountName does not change the common name, so the distinguished name remained CN=Jason Brooks,OU=HR,OU=Users,OU=GraceLab,DC=corp,DC=gracelab,DC=com.
Accidental deletion protection

A temporary Organizational Unit named TEMP-DeleteTest was created and a deletion deliberately attempted against it. A disposable object was used rather than a live Organizational Unit, because deleting one removes every object beneath it. Active Directory refused:

You do not have sufficient privileges to delete TEMP-DeleteTest,
or this object is protected from accidental deletion.

The message names two possible causes and gives no way to distinguish them. It also leads with the privileges explanation, which was not the cause, since the operation was performed as a member of Domain Admins. Diagnosis depended on inspecting the object rather than reading the error.

The Object tab confirmed the protection flag was set. Under the Advanced view of the Security tab the mechanism is visible: a Deny access control entry for Everyone on Delete and Delete Subtree. It is an access control entry rather than a console preference, which is why PowerShell enforces it identically.
PowerShell equivalent

Set-ADOrganizationalUnit -Identity "OU=TEMP-DeleteTest,OU=GraceLab,DC=corp,DC=gracelab,DC=com" `
    -ProtectedFromAccidentalDeletion $false
Remove-ADOrganizationalUnit -Identity "OU=TEMP-DeleteTest,OU=GraceLab,DC=corp,DC=gracelab,DC=com" -Confirm:$false
Security groups and AGDLP nesting
Three global groups hold departmental membership and one domain local group holds the permission on the shared resource.
PowerShell equivalent

$Groups = "OU=Groups,OU=GraceLab,DC=corp,DC=gracelab,DC=com"
"IT","HR","Sales" | ForEach-Object {
    New-ADGroup -Name "GG_$_" -GroupScope Global -GroupCategory Security -Path $Groups
}
New-ADGroup -Name "DL_SalesData_Modify" -GroupScope DomainLocal -GroupCategory Security -Path $Groups

Add-ADGroupMember -Identity "GG_IT"    -Members dcarter,ochen
Add-ADGroupMember -Identity "GG_HR"    -Members smitchell,jbrooks
Add-ADGroupMember -Identity "GG_Sales" -Members mreed,npatel
Add-ADGroupMember -Identity "DL_SalesData_Modify" -Members "GG_Sales"

Verification found a second defect. DL_SalesData_Modify had been created with Global scope, so the name asserted a scope the object did not hold and the intended chain was a global group nested inside another global group. The console had not revealed it, because its Type column was truncated to Security Group on every row.

Active Directory does not permit a direct conversion from Global to Domain Local, because the two scopes impose incompatible membership rules. The conversion was performed through Universal, which satisfies both.

Set-ADGroup -Identity "DL_SalesData_Modify" -GroupScope Universal
Set-ADGroup -Identity "DL_SalesData_Modify" -GroupScope DomainLocal
The conversion was possible because the group contains a global group and is not itself a member of any other group. A group nested elsewhere would have blocked it.
The resource and its NTFS permissions
A single shared folder was created so that the domain local group carries a real permission rather than existing as an unused object.

New-Item -Path "C:\Shares\SalesData" -ItemType Directory
New-SmbShare -Name "SalesData" -Path "C:\Shares\SalesData" -FullAccess "Authenticated Users"

icacls "C:\Shares\SalesData" /inheritance:d
icacls "C:\Shares\SalesData" /remove:g "BUILTIN\Users"
icacls "C:\Shares\SalesData" /grant "CORP\DL_SalesData_Modify:(OI)(CI)(M)"

The second and third commands carry the exercise. A folder created beneath the system drive inherits a read and execute entry for BUILTIN\Users, which every domain user holds through Authenticated Users. Granting Modify to the domain local group without first disabling inheritance and removing that entry would leave the folder readable by the whole domain, and the access control model would grant nothing that was not already there. Inherited entries cannot be removed while inheritance is enabled, so the flag is disabled first, which converts them to explicit entries.

Share permissions were deliberately left open to Authenticated Users. Effective access is the more restrictive of the share permission and the NTFS permission, so NTFS carries the whole model and there is one place to look when access is wrong. Restricting both layers at once is a common cause of effective permissions nobody can account for. In production this share would not sit on a domain controller; it does here because the lab has one server.
Workstation placement and redirection
CLIENT01 and CLIENT02 were placed in the default Computers container when they joined the domain in lab 06. Both objects were moved into the Workstations Organizational Unit.

Get-ADComputer CLIENT01 | Move-ADObject -TargetPath "OU=Workstations,OU=GraceLab,DC=corp,DC=gracelab,DC=com"
Get-ADComputer CLIENT02 | Move-ADObject -TargetPath "OU=Workstations,OU=GraceLab,DC=corp,DC=gracelab,DC=com"

Moving existing objects has no effect on where future objects are created. Any subsequent domain join would still land in the Computers container, which cannot be a Group Policy link target, so the domain default was redirected.
redircmp "OU=Workstations,OU=GraceLab,DC=corp,DC=gracelab,DC=com"

The command returned Redirection was successful. It updates the wellKnownObjects attribute on the domain object, which is why the result is observable through Get-ADDomain rather than only in the tool that set it.
RSAT on CLIENT01

External name resolution was tested from CLIENT01 before installing, because the Remote Server Administration Tools are a Feature on Demand retrieved from Windows Update and the installation fails without it.

Resolve-DnsName microsoft.com
Add-WindowsCapability -Online -Name Rsat.ActiveDirectory.DS-LDS.Tools~~~~0.0.1.0

The query returned A and AAAA records and no DNS forwarder was required. DC01 resolves external names through root hints by way of the VMware NAT gateway at 192.168.11.2, so the forwarder anticipated for this stage proved unnecessary. The installation returned Online: True and RestartNeeded: False.

Active Directory Users and Computers was then opened on CLIENT01 and connected to the domain. It was launched from a session whose hostname output had already been confirmed as CLIENT01, so there was no ambiguity about which machine the console was running on. The two virtual machines present near identical consoles, and the title bar names the domain controller answering the query rather than the machine running the tool.
Containers and Organizational Units are not interchangeable

The default Users and Computers objects are containers. A container cannot be the target of a Group Policy link and cannot receive delegated administrative control, which is the reason for building a custom hierarchy at all. The Type column states the object class in plain text and is a more reliable check than the icon. DC01 was left in the built-in Domain Controllers Organizational Unit, which is already an Organizational Unit and carries the Default Domain Controllers Policy.
The Disabled Users OU does not disable accounts

Moving an account into that Organizational Unit neither disables it nor prevents authentication. Disable-ADAccount is what stops an account from authenticating; the move is housekeeping performed afterwards.

The offboarding sequence is therefore to disable the account, verify the sign-in refusal at the client, move the object, then verify the new distinguished name. Verification sits between the two actions rather than after both, so that the refusal is attributable to the disable rather than to the move.
Naming standards need enforcing, not just defining

User sAMAccountName values use a lowercase first initial and surname with matching user principal names. Group names carry a scope prefix, GG_ for global groups holding accounts and DL_ for domain local groups holding permissions, so the access chain can be read from the names alone.

The convention collides at scale. A second Olivia Chen, or an Oscar Chen, both resolve to ochen. It is sufficient at lab scale; at production scale the usual remedies are a numeric suffix or a firstname.lastname form.

Two exceptions to the defined standards were found and corrected before dependent work continued: one sAMAccountName created in uppercase, and one group created with the wrong scope. Both were found because the build was verified rather than assumed complete, and neither was visible in the graphical console.
AGDLP separates membership from permission

Permissions were not assigned to individual users. Accounts go into a global group representing a role, the global group is nested into a domain local group representing access to a resource, and the domain local group receives the access control entry.
mreed, npatel  →  GG_Sales  →  DL_SalesData_Modify  →  Modify on C:\Shares\SalesData
Membership changes and permission changes then stay independent. A user moving into Sales is added to one group, and a change to what Sales may do on the folder alters one access control entry.
Inherited permissions decide who is denied

Assigning a permission establishes who is granted access. It does not establish who is denied. Disabling inheritance and removing the inherited BUILTIN\Users entry is what makes the denial real, and skipping it is the most common explanation for a departmental folder that everyone can open.
Group membership is evaluated at sign-in

Group membership is written into the user access token at sign-in. Adding a user to a group has no effect on their access until they sign out and back in, when a new token is issued. This is a frequent misdiagnosis on permission tickets: the change is correct, the symptom persists, and the corrective action is a sign out rather than a further permission change.
Moving objects and redirecting new objects are separate

Moving CLIENT01 and CLIENT02 organises two existing objects. Running redircmp changes where future domain joined computers are created, so new machines land in a Group Policy targetable Organizational Unit without manual intervention. The two operations address different problems and both are required.

A computer object move takes effect immediately in the directory, but computer configuration policy is read at startup, so a Group Policy Object linked to the Workstations Organizational Unit does not apply to either client until it restarts or refreshes policy.
Remote administration does not require console access to a DC

With RSAT installed on CLIENT01, the console runs on the workstation and queries DC01 over the network. The title bar reads DC01.corp.gracelab.com, which names the domain controller answering the query rather than the machine running the console, so the title alone does not establish where administration is happening.

The account used here is a member of Domain Admins, which is appropriate for building an environment and not for routine help desk work. Delegating specific rights over specific Organizational Units, such as password resets confined to a departmental Organizational Unit, is the model this structure is built to support.

Get-ADOrganizationalUnit -Filter * -SearchBase "OU=GraceLab,DC=corp,DC=gracelab,DC=com" |
    Select-Object Name,DistinguishedName | Sort-Object DistinguishedName

Get-ADUser -Filter * -SearchBase "OU=Users,OU=GraceLab,DC=corp,DC=gracelab,DC=com" `
    -Properties UserPrincipalName | Select-Object Name,SamAccountName,UserPrincipalName

Get-ADGroup -Filter * -SearchBase "OU=Groups,OU=GraceLab,DC=corp,DC=gracelab,DC=com" |
    Select-Object Name,GroupScope,GroupCategory

icacls "C:\Shares\SalesData"

Get-ADComputer -Filter * | Select-Object Name,DistinguishedName
Get-ADDomain | Select-Object ComputersContainer

Sorting Organizational Units by distinguished name orders them by position in the tree, because a distinguished name reads from the object outwards to the domain and siblings share a common suffix. The nesting row is the one worth reading twice: the domain local group returns a single member whose objectClass is group rather than user, which is the AGDLP relationship itself rather than an inference from the group name.
Sales users reach the folder through the group chain. A user outside it, such as jbrooks, holds no entry at any level and is denied.
